newsitem.title: FRANCE: Russia's Dubinin optimistic on IMF loan.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Dubinin optimistic on IMF loan.

text.p: Russian central bank chief Sergei Dubinin said on Wednesday he was convinced Moscow would be able to meet targets on improving tax collection -- a condition for renewing disbursements of an International Monetary Fund loan.
"I am convinced the objectives will be met," he told a bankers conference in Paris.
Dubinin, speaking in Russian through a French interpreter, also said he thought Russian economic growth would be at least flat next year after shrinking this year.
Tax collection was a key problem for Russia, and Moscow was determined to make a major effort in the months ahead to improve it and provide resources for its budget, he said.
"We are going to adopt much stricter rules on tax collection," he said.
Disbursements on the three-year, $10 billion International Monetary Fund loan have been held up, partly because of IMF worries about tax revenues.
But Dubinin later told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV) in an interview that the chances of obtaining a new tranche of IMF funds had improved.
"Our chances to receive the new tranche are better in November than October," he said in the interview.
"We hope that the monthly examination in November will be passed and we will be able to met these objectives, and therefore the (IMF) tranches will be paid in time," he told the conference.
Dubinin also said the economy would improve next year after a shrinkage of around five percent in 1996.
"We hope to see a reversal in that trend in 1997... to obtain at least zero percent," he said, adding this would be mainly due to exports.

He said Russia planned to continue its policy of regulating the exchange rate of the rouble to avoid excessive fluctuations. "Exchange rate policy will be in line with what was done over the last two years, with a few small modifications," he said.
In his RFTV interview he said that a decree would be issued before December 1 on regulating the exchange rate.

He also said that the members of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) should take inspiration from western Europe and coordinate their exchange rate policies rather than let the situation deteriorate into a currency war.
"We are more and more convinced that we must coordinate exchange rate policy," he said.
